description.summary: A Hellenistic Greek hand-powered geared device, recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, that calculated and displayed astronomical positions, eclipse cycles, and the four-year cycle of athletic games.
description.full: The Antikythera Mechanism is a hand-powered geared device of Hellenistic Greek manufacture, dated to the 2nd or early 1st century BCE, recovered in 1900–1901 from the wreck of a cargo ship off the island of Antikythera in the southern Aegean. The mechanism survives in 82 corroded bronze fragments and is held by the National Archaeological Museum of Athens. It originally consisted of a wooden box approximately 34 × 18 × 9 cm housing at least 30 interlocking bronze gears with hand-cut triangular teeth. Operated by a hand crank, the device modelled the motions of the Sun and Moon, predicted lunar and solar eclipses through the Saros cycle, tracked the 19-year Metonic cycle, displayed the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games on a dedicated dial, and is now believed to have indicated the positions of the five planets known to antiquity. Modern study began with Derek J. de Solla Price's pioneering 1959 and 1974 work and has been transformed since 2005 by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which used high-resolution X-ray computed tomography (Bladed Surface Imaging at X-Tek) to read the inscriptions hidden in the corroded fragments. The mechanism stands as the earliest known geared analog computer and the most sophisticated surviving piece of Hellenistic mechanical technology.

etymology.origin: Named after the Greek island of Antikythera (Αντικύθηρα), off whose coast the wreck was discovered.
etymology.meaning: 'Antikythera' means 'opposite Kythera', i.e. the island opposite Kythera (Cythera).
etymology.first_use: The artifact was first identified as something more than ordinary corroded bronze on 17 May 1902, when archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear embedded in one of the fragments.

features.description: At least 30 surviving bronze gears with hand-cut triangular teeth

features.feature: Front dial — zodiac and Egyptian calendar
features.description: Concentric dials marking the 360-degree zodiac and the 365-day Egyptian calendar

features.feature: Back dials — Metonic, Saros, Olympic, Callippic, Exeligmos
features.description: Spiral back dials tracking long-period astronomical and games cycles
Greek inscriptions on the dial plates (the 'instruction manual'), now read via CT imaging

physical.morphology: A box-mounted geared analog computer, hand-cranked, with front and back dials and concentric pointers.

abilities.description: Tracks the 223-month Saros cycle to predict solar and lunar eclipses
Models the 19-year Metonic cycle reconciling lunar and solar calendars
Indicates the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games (revealed by Freeth et al. 2008)
Models the irregular motion of the Moon using a pin-and-slot mechanism (Freeth et al. 2006)
Reconstructions including Freeth & Jones (2012) and the 2021 UCL model argue for indication of the five classical planets

range.description: A unique surviving artifact, currently held in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens; recovered from the seafloor off Antikythera, Greece.

hotspots.name: Antikythera shipwreck site

location.description: Seafloor off Pinakakia point, northeast coast of Antikythera

hotspots.notes: Discovered by Symiote sponge divers led by Captain Dimitrios Kontos.

location.description: Permanent home of the 82 surviving fragments

first_recorded.source: Discovery by Symiote sponge divers off Antikythera

peak_activity_periods.description: Pioneering study by Derek J. de Solla Price
Antikythera Mechanism Research Project: high-resolution X-ray CT imaging and inscription reading

origins.cultural_roots: Hellenistic Greek mathematical astronomy, plausibly within the tradition associated with figures such as Hipparchus and the Posidonian school.
origins.earliest_accounts: The mechanism itself is the primary evidence; literary references to similar geared 'spheres' appear in Cicero (De Re Publica) describing devices made by Archimedes.
origins.folklore_connections: Has become a touchstone in modern 'ancient mystery' literature, often invoked as evidence of unexpectedly advanced ancient technology.

timeline.event: Sponge divers under Captain Dimitrios Kontos discover the Antikythera shipwreck off Antikythera
Mechanism fragments are recovered from the wreck during a Greek government salvage operation
timeline.significance: Recovery of the mechanism's surviving fragments

timeline.event: Archaeologist Valerios Stais identifies a gear embedded in one of the corroded fragments
timeline.significance: First recognition that the object is mechanical
timeline.source: Stais (1902) report to the Athens Archaeological Society

timeline.event: Derek J. de Solla Price publishes 'An Ancient Greek Computer' in Scientific American
Price publishes 'Gears from the Greeks' in Trans. Am. Phil. Soc.
timeline.source: Price, D. (1974), Trans. Am. Phil. Soc. 64(7)

timeline.event: Freeth et al. publish 'Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism' in Nature
timeline.significance: Reveals 37-gear scheme and lunar anomaly mechanism via X-ray CT

timeline.event: Freeth et al. publish in Nature on the Olympiad / games dial
timeline.significance: Identifies the Panhellenic games dial on the back of the mechanism

timeline.event: UCL Antikythera Research Team publish 'A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism' in Scientific Reports
timeline.significance: Comprehensive proposed reconstruction of the front cosmos display including all five planets

history.modern_era: The mechanism is the subject of an ongoing international research programme combining Greek archaeology, X-ray computed tomography, epigraphy, and the history of astronomy. Multiple working physical reconstructions have been built (Wright; Freeth & Jones; Edmunds team; Hublot watchmaking models).

physical.name: Antikythera Mechanism fragments
physical.description: 82 surviving bronze and wood fragments of the original device, currently inventoried in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens.
physical.analysis: Subjected to X-ray microfocus CT imaging by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project from 2005 onward; inscriptions and gear teeth read in unprecedented detail.

scientific.name: Hellenistic geared astronomical instrument
scientific.description: The mainstream consensus: the mechanism is a 2nd-century BCE Hellenistic Greek astronomical computer, the product of an unbroken tradition of geared mechanical astronomy that has otherwise left only literary traces (Cicero on Archimedes' sphere).
evidence_cited: Astronomical content matching known Hellenistic models

skeptical.name: Rejection of 'lost civilisation' framings
skeptical.description: Mainstream historians of science reject popular framings of the mechanism as evidence of a 'lost civilisation' or extraterrestrial intervention; the device is fully explicable within Hellenistic Greek mathematical astronomy.

folklore.beliefs: The mechanism is widely (and largely incorrectly) cited in popular 'ancient technology' discourse as anomalous; among historians of science it is celebrated as a remarkable but contextually intelligible artifact.
